note: Track guitar-melodies (guitar-scales), step 4: a tune that leaves one position and shifts to the next, then the same tune in other keys and a tune that comes down the whole neck. missing: the melody shape takes no position, so the tab decides where the shift falls and nothing marks it on the neck.

exercise.title: A tune that shifts position
exercise.why: A tune that climbs past the top of one position needs the next one, so you move your whole hand on one note and let the fingers fall on new frets.

cells.text:
The neck below frames two positions of A major that sit side by side. Press Play below to hear the framed notes run up and back down, then play them yourself.
Keep going until you can see where the lower position ends and the upper one starts.

Press Play below to start the backing, and play the tune from the tab. Most of it sits in the lower position: where the tab climbs the high e string, move your whole hand up and keep one finger to a fret.
Once the shift lands on the beat, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the backing again.
If the shift comes late, go back a stage and play the tune there.

Press Play below to start the backing, and play the same tune again.
Then play it in another key. Use the Key selector below to change the key, then press Play to start the backing again.
When you change the key, the tune keeps its shape, but the shift can fall on another note: find it in the tab before you play.

Press Play below to start the backing. This tune starts high and comes down the neck, so your hand shifts more than once.
Before each shift, look at the fret you are going to and not at your hand.
